card: Paper card. Question: How can the design principles of metastable β-Ti alloys be converged with high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys to achieve both high yield strength and low elastic modulus for biomedical implants?. System: Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo, Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta, Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta, Ti-V-Mo, Ti-V-Zr-Mo, and Ti-rich variants (e.g., Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5, Ti35-Zr27.5-Hf27.5-Nb5-Ta5). Processing: Casting (as-cast), annealing (e.g., 1000 °C for 168 h), and thermodynamic simulation using FactSage, Pandat, and Thermo-Calc to adjust compositions for phase stability and segregation reduction. Test conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in simulated body fluid, compression and tensile testing, cell culture tests (osteoblasts), X-ray diffraction (XRD), SAED-TEM, and EPMA-WDS mapping. Findings: Equiatomic Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo HEA exhibited a compressive yield strength of 1330 MPa but suffered from severe dendritic segregation and a high elastic modulus.; Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta MEA (quaternary) achieved a compressive strain of 48 ± 6% and yield strength >1000 MPa, surpassing Ti-6Al-4V (970 MPa).; Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5 alloy showed the lowest elastic modulus (86 GPa) among Ti-rich MEAs and a yield strength of 1381 MPa.; Metastable Ti65-Zr18-Nb16-Mo1 ([Mo]eq ≈ 10) achieved high yield strength (>1100 MPa) and a lower elastic modulus (~60 GPa).; Ti45-Zr45-Nb5-Ta5 MEA (VEC = 4.18) exhibited a low elastic modulus of 57 GPa.; Increasing Ti content in Tix-Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs increased yield strength by 31% (Ti1 vs Ti0.25) and improved compressive deformability.; Ti1.4-Zr1.4-Nb0.6-Ta0.6-Mo0.6 HEA showed osteoblasts with more pseudopodia and longer focal adhesions compared to commercially pure Ti.. Mechanism: The authors argue that reducing the valence electron concentration (VEC) to 4.0–4.2 or the Mo equivalent ([Mo]eq) to below 10 wt% induces a metastable β-phase, which lowers the elastic modulus. Simultaneously, the high-entropy effects (lattice distortion, solid solution strengthening) and Ti-rich compositions enhance yield strength. Reducing the atomic size misfit (δ) and mixing enthalpy (ΔHmix) near zero minimizes compositional segregation and prevents intermetallic formation, thereby improving ductility and corrosion resistance.. Limitations: Severe compositional segregation persists in many equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs/MEAs, leading to high elastic modulus, reduced ductility, and decreased corrosion resistance. The Ms theory may not be applicable to HEAs/MEAs, and some alloys with high Ti content still exhibit segregation. The presence of Laves phases or secondary BCC phases can adversely affect mechanical properties.. Future work: Developing metastable β HEAs/MEAs that combine high strength and low modulus; surface modification of Ti-containing HEAs to induce bioactivity (e.g., anodization, hydroxyapatite deposition); further investigation into the relationship between thermodynamic parameters and modulus; and reducing segregation through optimized composition design.. Quote: "To satisfy the demands of biomedical implants, researchers have sought to synthesize the strengths of high-entropy alloys and metastable β-Ti alloys, culminating in the development of metastable high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys that manifest both high strength and a low elastic modulus."

card: Paper card. Question: How to rapidly design low-cost Co-free Al-Cr-Fe-Ni FCC/B2-structured eutectic medium entropy alloys (EMEAs) with excellent mechanical and corrosion properties?. System: Al-Cr-Fe-Ni system, specifically AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 and AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5 alloys. Processing: Vacuum arc melting under pure argon atmosphere; raw materials >99.9 wt% purity; remelted at least five times; solidified in a water-cooled copper hearth (18 mm diameter, 12 mm thickness). Test conditions: Compressive tests at 1 × 10−3 s−1 strain rate; electrochemical tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 °C; potentiodynamic polarization scan rate 1 mV/min; EIS from 105 to 10−2 Hz. Findings: Mathematical rules established: c ≥ 1.0, 4.38a + 4.28b + 3.97c ≈ 20.55, and c − a ˃ 1.0.; Both alloys exhibit lamellar eutectic microstructure with FCC and ordered B2 (B2) phases.; Volume ratio of B2 to FCC phase (VB2/VFCC) is 0.605 for AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 and 0.679 for AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5.; Yield stress higher than 500 MPa and compressive fracture strength higher than 2450 MPa.; Fracture strain > 40% for both alloys.; AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 shows better corrosion resistance with Ecorr of −436 mV and Icorr of 7.42 μA∙cm−2.; Cr-rich spherical nanoparticles segregate within the B2 phase matrix.; L12 nanoprecipitates are found within the FCC phase of AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5.. Mechanism: The unique lamellar microstructure allows coordinated deformation: soft FCC phase undergoes initial plastic deformation while hard B2 phase remains elastic, piling up dislocations at interfaces; Cr-rich BCC nanoprecipitates further hinder dislocation movement, improving strength and strain-hardening. Better corrosion resistance in AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 is attributed to the higher volume fraction of the FCC phase and higher nickel content.. Limitations: The text notes that traditional trial-and-error methods are time-consuming and have low success rates, though the proposed rule addresses this; no specific limitations of the current study's results are explicitly stated by the authors beyond the general challenge of industrial application for Co-containing alloys which this work aims to solve.. Future work: The authors state that the established rule has great potential in the composition design of EHEAs and imply further application of this rule to design more alloys, but do not explicitly list specific future experiments in the 'future work' section.. Quote: "The mathematical formulas are c ≥ 1.0, 4.38a + 4.28b + 3.97c ≈ 20.55, and c − a ˃ 1.0."
W4312187064.title: Rapid Design, Microstructures, and Properties of Low-Cost Co-Free Al-Cr-Fe-Ni Eutectic Medium Entropy Alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How does substituting Cr with V to tune atomic volume misfit affect the magnetic order and electric transport properties (specifically strange metallicity) in the CoNi(Cr/V) medium-entropy alloy system?. System: Ternary equiatomic CoNiCr (CNC), CoNi(Cr0.5V0.5) (CNCV), and CoNiV (CNV) medium-entropy alloys. Processing: Arc melting of high-purity elements, homogenization at 1100 °C for 24 hrs in Ar followed by water quenching, cold rolling to ~75% thickness reduction, and solutionizing at 1000 °C for 60 min followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Magnetization and electrical transport measurements performed in the temperature range of 5–335 K using a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) and 4-probe method. Findings: All three compositions exhibited a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure with lattice parameters of 3.576 ± 0.004 Å (CNC), 3.598 ± 0.002 Å (CNCV), and 3.617 ± 0.002 Å (CNV).; Magnetic moments at 5 K were extremely small: 0.005 μB/f.u. for CNC, 0.007 μB/f.u. for CNCV, and 0.002 μB/f.u. for CNV.; The CoNiCr system displayed linear temperature dependence of resistivity (ρ(T) = ρ0 + ρ1 T), indicative of strange metallicity.; Vanadium-substituted samples (CNCV and CNV) required an additional electron-electron scattering term (ρ2 T2) to fit resistivity data, suggesting a deviation from pure quantum criticality.; Coercive fields for all alloys ranged from 30 to 60 Gauss (2.4–4.8 kA/m), classifying them as semihard magnets.; Residual resistivity ratio (RRR) monotonically decreased with increasing Vanadium substitution, indicating higher residual resistivity.; No significant magnetoresistance was observed in any of the samples.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the small magnetic moments and strange metallicity to magnetically driven chemical short-range order (SRO) and magnetic frustration. They propose that complex interactions between ferromagnetic Co/Ni and antiferromagnetic Cr/V create unbalanced magnetic sublattices (ferrimagnetism), where the frustration of magnetic moments leads to the observed linear resistivity and quantum critical behavior.. Limitations: The ferrimagnetic Curie temperature was not determined due to setup limitations preventing high-temperature measurements, and the authors note that direct experimental evidence of SRO remains intangible without advanced tools like muon spin resonance.. Future work: The authors suggest that careful experimental tools such as muon spin resonance and/or neutron reflectivity are needed to shed light on the magnetic short-range order driven by a state of frustration.. Quote: "The electric transport measurements revealed a strange metallicity evidenced through the observation of the linear temperature dependence of the resistivity."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the biocompatibility of a Ti-rich medium-entropy alloy (Ti65M) compare to a Ti-alloy (TNSM) and commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti) regarding glioblastoma astrocytoma cell viability, morphology, and gene expression?. System: Ti65-Zr18-Nb16-Mo1 (Ti65M), Ti-13Nb-7Sn-4Mo (TNSM), and commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti). Processing: Arc-melting and casting system (A-028, Dawn Shine, New Taipei City, Taiwan); samples cut into discs (10 mm diameter, 1 mm height); surfaces abraded to #1500 silicon carbide papers; cleaned ultrasonically with alcohol, acetone, and deionized water. Test conditions: U-87 MG glioblastoma astrocytoma cells (1 × 10^4 cells) seeded on 1.2 cm diameter samples; incubated for 24 h, then replated for an additional 24 h prior to MTT tests; extracts tested via PBS wash; contact angles measured with 1μL deionized water; XRD (40 kV, 40 mA, 2θ = 20–90°); AFM (5 × 5 μm2 scanning range). Findings: Ti65M exhibited the highest hardness (366.5 ± 3.6 HV) and lowest average roughness (38 ± 8 nm), while CP-Ti had the lowest hardness (172.3 ± 4.4 HV) and highest roughness (94 ± 26 nm).; All three materials were hydrophilic, with CP-Ti having the lowest contact angle (46.0 ± 0.9°) compared to Ti65M (54.3 ± 2.0°).; Cell viability on Ti65M and TNSM (β structures) was considerably higher than on CP-Ti (α' structure), with viability decreasing as Ti content increased.; U-87 MG cells showed the highest number of dendrites and axons on Ti65M, with significantly fewer observed on TNSM and CP-Ti.; Expression of ERK was reduced on TNSM and CP-Ti substrates compared to Ti65M, potentially causing lower cell migration and proliferation.; Higher expression of p53 and NFkβ was observed in U-87 MG cells on CP-Ti compared to other alloys, suggesting CP-Ti may induce apoptosis.; All extract viabilities exceeded 90%, indicating low indirect cytotoxicity for all three materials.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the superior biocompatibility of Ti65M is related to its high content of Zr and Nb elements, which are highly biocompatible and exhibit low cytotoxicity. Additionally, the metastable β-phase structure and high hardness improve wear resistance, preventing accelerated release of metal ions. The lower expression of p53 on Ti65M compared to CP-Ti suggests reduced apoptosis, while higher expression of growth factor pathway genes (RAS, ERK, S6) on Ti65M correlates with increased cell growth and migration.. Limitations: The authors state that the mechanisms connecting surface roughness and hydrophilicity to cellular adhesion, growth, autophagy, and differentiation are not yet clear. They also note that phase structure alone is insufficient to explain viability differences and that further investigation of corrosion resistance is needed.. Future work: The authors propose that increased cell migration on Ti65M is a subject for further study and that further investigation of the corrosion resistance of Ti65M and TNSM will be reported in future studies.. Quote: "Ti65M has an ultra-low elastic modulus (61 GPa) due to its metastable state, which is significantly lower than those of Ti-64 (110 GPa) [] and TZNTM HEA (153 GPa) []."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase high-entropy intermetallic alloy be designed to overcome the inherent brittleness of traditional intermetallics and achieve both high strength and extensive plasticity at room temperature and high homologous temperatures?. System: (CoNi)50(TiZrHf)50 (at. %) single-phase B2 high-entropy intermetallic alloy. Processing: Arc-melting high-purity raw materials (>99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, remelted at least five times, drop-cast into a copper mold, homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h, and water quenched. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression from room temperature to ~0.9Tm (1582 K) at 1 × 10−3 s−1; microcompression on 1 μm diameter pillars at RT, 573 K, and 673 K; in situ STEM at RT and 573 K. Findings: Yield strength of ~1.5 GPa with plastic strain of ~8% at room temperature, which is about eight times that of conventional B2 alloys like NiAl and CoTi.; The alloy exhibits no precipitous thermal softening between homologous temperatures of 0.5 and 0.7, maintaining strength and strain hardening up to ~0.7Tm.; Micropillars with [100], [110], and [111] orientations show similar yield strength and elastic stiffness, indicating isotropic-like mechanical behavior.; Two slip systems, {110}<111> and {010}<100>, were identified with critical resolved shear stresses of 1235 ± 39 MPa and 1176 ± 245 MPa, respectively, differing by only 5%.; At room temperature, deformation induces local amorphization within slip bands, whereas at temperatures above 573 K, deformation results in dense dislocation forests without amorphization.; The velocity ratio of screw-to-edge dislocations was calculated to be ~0.6 at 300 K, significantly higher than the ~0.2 ratio in brittle BCC metals like tungsten.. Mechanism: Severe lattice distortion caused by atomic size and electronic property misfit mitigates atomic bonding differences along various crystal orientations, enabling dislocation multiplicity and isotropic behavior. Dislocation gliding disturbs the local chemical order, causing structural instability that leads to amorphization at low temperatures and the formation of local crystal-like order (dynamic hardening) at high temperatures, which impedes subsequent dislocation gliding and stabilizes plastic flow.. Limitations: The text notes that fracture at low temperatures may occur within amorphized regions and that the plastic strain at room temperature can vary (up to 27%) depending on machine stiffness, though this variability disappears at higher temperatures.. Future work: The authors suggest that manipulating the lattice distortion by adjusting the ratio of Co to Ni is a topic that warrants further research but is out of the scope of the current work.. Quote: "Unlike conventional intermetallics, this high-entropy alloy features a highly distorted crystalline lattice with complex chemical order, leading to multiple slip systems and high flow stress."

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the mobility mechanisms of screw and edge dislocations in the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) across a wide temperature range?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), specifically comparing random solid solution (RSS) and equilibrium SRO states at 800 K. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a moment tensor potential (MTP) machine-learning interatomic potential; SRO states equilibrated via hybrid MD/Monte Carlo (MD/MC) approach at 800 K. Test conditions: Temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K; applied shear stresses ranging from 0 to 3.0 GPa for screws and 0 to 1.0 GPa for edges; dislocation line length ~15 nm. Findings: At 300 K, SRO provides an extra strengthening of ~180 MPa for screw dislocations due to the formation of diffuse antiphase boundaries (DAPBs).; The strengthening effect of SRO on screw dislocations attenuates with increasing temperature, becoming negligible at 2000 K where mobility curves for RSS and SRO samples overlap.; A cross-slip locking mechanism involving the formation of jogs is observed for screw dislocations, providing extra strengthening independent of SRO presence.; Unlike screw dislocations, the mobility of edge dislocations is enhanced by the presence of SRO, particularly in the high-stress regime.; The SRO-induced enhancement of edge dislocation mobility extends to a characteristic length scale of approximately 1.2 nm into neighboring planes.; At 300 K, dislocation velocities in the MoNbTaW RHEA are significantly lower than in pure Mo and Nb, but this difference diminishes at 2000 K.; The attenuation of SRO strengthening at high temperatures is attributed to the increasing contribution of the entropy term (ΔS_kp) to the kink-pair formation free energy.. Mechanism: For screw dislocations, SRO creates an energy barrier (DAPB formation energy) that must be overcome during kink-pair nucleation, causing strengthening that is thermally activated and thus diminishes at high temperatures. For edge dislocations, SRO flattens the energy landscape, reducing solute drag effects and enhancing mobility despite the energy cost of disrupting order on the slip plane. Cross-slip locking in screws involves the formation of jogs on different slip planes that pin the dislocation line.. Limitations: The simulations use short dislocation line lengths (~15 nm) compared to realistic experimental conditions, meaning calculated velocities are dependent on this size and cannot be directly compared to macroscopic theoretical models without extrapolation. The study assumes the SRO state remains fixed during dislocation motion and does not account for changes in ordering around the moving core.. Future work: The authors state that predicting how the identified mechanisms combine to determine material strength requires appealing to mesoscale models for longer dislocation lengths and longer timescales, which is beyond the scope of the current work.. Quote: "The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced."

Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) and temperature affect the mobility and friction stress of edge versus screw dislocations in a bcc MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) compared to pure bcc metals and binary alloys?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), pure Mo, and binary Mo-Nb alloys (Mo95Nb5 to Mo75Nb25). Processing: Machine-learning interatomic potential (MTP) with radius cutoff (Rcut) of 4.7 Å and maximum level (levmax) of 14; MC/MD equilibration at 800 K; dislocation mobility simulations using LAMMPS with shear stress ramped at 20 MPa per 1.5 ps and held for 150 ps at temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K. Test conditions: Temperatures: 300 K and 2000 K; Shear stress ramp rate: 20 MPa per 1.5 ps; Hold time: 150 ps; Critical friction stress defined at 0.2 Å/ps for screw and 1.0 Å/ps for edge dislocations. Findings: The edge-to-screw velocity ratio decreases from 20 at 300 K to 11 at 2000 K in MoNbTaW.; Critical friction stress for edge dislocations decreases by 140 MPa from 300 to 2000 K.; Critical friction stress for screw dislocations decreases by 1.3 GPa (an order of magnitude larger) from 300 to 2000 K.; At ~2000 K, the critical friction stresses for both edge and screw dislocations decay to approximately the same level.; SRO hinders screw dislocation motion but accelerates edge dislocation motion in the RHEA.; A novel cross-slip locking mechanism was observed in the RHEA, attributed to intrinsic energy fluctuations and rugged energy landscapes.; Critical stress for screw dislocations follows an exponential decay with temperature, while edge dislocations follow a linear decrease.; Binary Mo-Nb alloys show lower critical friction stresses compared to the RHEA, with edge friction converging to zero in pure bcc metals.. Mechanism: Screw dislocations move via kink-pair nucleation and migration; SRO increases the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation, causing temperature-dependent strengthening. Edge dislocations are accelerated by SRO through the attenuation of solute interaction magnitudes. The cross-slip locking mechanism arises from intrinsic energy fluctuations along the dislocation line and the rugged energy landscape.. Limitations: The study notes that the cross-slip locking mechanism was observed even with a limited cell size, implying potential size effects, and the phenomenological model is constructed specifically for the double-kink mechanism.. Future work: The authors state that the findings demonstrate mechanisms that can have a significant impact on mechanical properties, implying future work should explore these impacts, though no specific future experiments are explicitly detailed in the provided text.. Quote: "The edge-to-screw mobility ratio is around 20 at 300 K, which decreases to 11 when the temperature is raised to 2000 K."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the physical origins of the exceptional high-temperature strength and strength retention in refractory body-centered-cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs)?. System: NbTaTiV (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at.%) and CrMoNbV (nominal CrMoNbV at.%); search space includes the 10-component Al-Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr family.. Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt.% purity elements under argon atmosphere followed by drop-casting into cylindrical rods; NbTaTiV homogenized at 1473 K for 3 days then water-cooled; CrMoNbV tested in the as-cast state.. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at strain rates of 1 × 10−3 s−1 (NbTaTiV) and 2 × 10−4 s−1 (CrMoNbV); temperatures up to 1173 K; in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) performed during deformation.. Findings: Neutron diffraction peak broadening analysis yielded q values of -0.6 to -0.4 for NbTaTiV and -2 for CrMoNbV, consistent with edge dislocations and distinct from screw dislocations (+1.9 to +2.1).; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of NbTaTiV deformed at 293 K showed 75% (58 of 77) of dislocations were of edge character.; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of CrMoNbV deformed at 293 K showed 56% (23 of 41) of dislocations were of edge character.; At 1173 K, edge dislocations remained dominant with 82% (27 of 33) in NbTaTiV and 64% (81 of 127) in CrMoNbV.; The CrMoNbV alloy exhibited the highest reported strength at a homologous temperature of 1173 K.; A computationally guided search over 10^7 BCC HEA compositions identified over 10^6 possible ultra-strong high-temperature alloy compositions.; Theoretical predictions for NbTaTiV strength were lower than experimental values by ~300-500 MPa, attributed to 1.6 at.% O+N interstitial impurities.. Mechanism: In complex HEAs, fluctuations in local solute arrangements create large local variations in potential energy, forcing edge dislocations to adopt a low-energy wavy structure; plastic flow requires thermal activation to overcome large energy barriers created by adjacent high-energy environments, enabling high strength retention at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The theory does not capture the strength plateau observed at 973–1273 K in many BCC HEAs; neutron pattern quality for CrMoNbV was lower than for NbTaTiV, especially at low plastic strains; the theory assumes a homogeneous average alloy which may not fully capture local complexities.. Future work: Propose fabrication and testing of specific alloys (Mo5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo2.5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo6WCrZrHf, Mo2.5TaWV2.5CrZrHf) with predicted strengths of ~2.5-3 GPa at 1300 K; combine design strategy with detailed thermodynamics and high ductility criteria to discover multi-objective alloys.. Quote: "Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations."

card: Paper card. Question: How does temperature influence the transition between smooth (mild) and intermittent (wild) plastic flow in body-centered cubic (bcc) Niobium, and what is the underlying dislocation mechanism governing this bimodal behavior?. System: Single-crystal Niobium (Nb), commercially pure, oriented along the ⟨123⟩ direction. Processing: Focused ion beam (FIB) milling to fabricate cylindrical microcrystals (height 6 μm, diameter 2 μm); uniaxial microcompression testing at a displacement rate of 0.6 nm s⁻¹ (strain rate 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) across temperatures of 173–368 K; 3D discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) simulations using the MODELib package at strain rates of 718 s⁻¹ and 7180 s⁻¹. Test conditions: Temperatures: 173 K, 263 K, 298 K, 323 K, 368 K; Strain rates: 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (experiment), 718 s⁻¹ and 7180 s⁻¹ (simulation); Loading axis: ⟨123⟩; Slip system: {211}⟨111⟩. Findings: Plasticity is bimodal, consisting of thermally activated smooth flow ('mild') and athermal intermittent bursts ('wild') that coexist across the temperature regime.; The effective barrier energy for athermal dislocation avalanches is 0.04 eV, which is an order of magnitude smaller than the 0.3 eV barrier energy for smooth plastic flow at 298 K.; The distribution of avalanche sizes shifts from a scale-free power law at 298–368 K to an exponential (Weibull) distribution at 173 K, with a characteristic length scale of ~0.3 nm.; The fraction of athermal slip activity (η) increases markedly at the critical temperature Tc (approx. 290–320 K), where screw and edge dislocation mobilities equalize.; DDD simulations confirm that screw dislocations are the dominant segment type (>90%) in avalanches, despite the observed athermal behavior.; Screw dislocations involved in avalanches are subjected to local stresses significantly exceeding the Peierls stress (τ > τP), neutralizing their thermal sensitivity.; The proportion of athermal strain contribution decreases with decreasing temperature due to a reduction in the effective screening length for elastic coupling.. Mechanism: The authors argue that athermal screw dislocation slip is driven by the emergence of local stresses in screw dislocation pileups that exceed the Peierls stress (τP). When τ > τP, screw dislocations exhibit viscous motion similar to edge dislocations, effectively bypassing the classical thermally activated kink-pair nucleation mechanism. As temperature decreases, the Peierls potential increases, reducing the 'screening distance' (2d0) for elastic coupling between dislocations, which suppresses the length scale of avalanches and transitions the statistics from scale-free to exponential.. Limitations: The experimental sensor resolution limits the ability to detect rearrangements smaller than the current noise threshold (~0.165 nm), preventing observation of potential single-armed spiral source activity at very low temperatures. Additionally, the DDD simulations were performed at strain rates (718 s⁻¹) much higher than experimental rates (10⁻⁴ s⁻¹), though the authors note the strain-rate sensitivity exponents match.. Future work: The authors suggest that verifying the activity of single-armed spiral sources at very low temperatures would require nanomechanical testing with displacement resolution higher than current state-of-the-art capabilities. They also propose that the ratio of athermal to total plastic strain (η) could serve as a direct experimental method to determine the critical temperature Tc.. Quote: "Plasticity is shown to be bimodal across the studied temperature regime, with conventional thermally-activated smooth plastic flow ('mild') coexisting with sporadic bursts ('wild') controlled by athermal screw dislocation activity."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the intrinsic lattice response of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to external stimuli when pre-existing defects like dislocations are minimized, and does this lead to a new form of elastic instability?. System: Nanoscale BCC-structured high-entropy alloys: TiHfZrNb (quaternary), TiHfZrNbTa (quinary), TiZrNb (ternary), and binary ZrNb; compared with elemental Nb and FCC HEAs (FeCoNiCrCu, FeCoNiCrMn). Processing: Alloys prepared by vacuum arc melting (8+ remelts); nanoscale dog-bone samples synthesized via in situ welding in TEM using square electric pulses (1 ms duration, 0-2 V voltage); samples stretched quasi-statically at a strain rate of ∽10⁻³ s⁻¹. Test conditions: In situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) under uniaxial tensile loading along [001] and <110> directions; temperature 300 K; electron beam effects verified as negligible. Findings: Nanoscale BCC HEAs (ternary, quaternary, quinary) undergo elastic strain-induced amorphization at a critical elastic strain of ∽10% without dislocation generation.; The initial BCC lattice elongates into a low-symmetry body-centered tetragonal (BCT) structure before amorphization, with ∽10% elongation along the loading axis and ∽3% lateral contraction.; Binary ZrNb and elemental Nb samples do not exhibit amorphization; instead, they undergo dislocation slip or phase transformation (BCC to FCC) at a lower critical strain of ∽4%.; FCC-structured HEAs (FeCoNiCrCu, FeCoNiCrMn) show dislocation-mediated elastic instability rather than amorphization.; The transition from crystalline to amorphous structure involves a diffusive interface with a transition layer of ∽1.5 nm containing a highly distorted lattice.; Atomic-resolution EDX mapping reveals incipient concentration waves with clustering length scales of ∽2–3 nm in ternary TiZrNb, indicating strong local chemical inhomogeneity.; First-principles and MD simulations confirm that local atomic environment inhomogeneity raises the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation, allowing large elastic strains to accumulate.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the phenomenon to the severe local atomic environment inhomogeneity in HEAs caused by multiple principal elements. This inhomogeneity creates 'hot spots' with varying local atomic displacements, which dramatically reduces the effective volume for dislocation nucleation (N). Consequently, the critical elastic shear strain for dislocation nucleation is significantly increased, preventing premature plastic relaxation. This allows the lattice to sustain elastic strains up to ∽10%, at which point the elastic strain energy overcomes the energy barrier between the crystalline and amorphous structures, triggering instantaneous amorphization.. Limitations: The lack of in situ tensile curves limits the understanding of the role of mechanical-driven amorphization in the macroscopic mechanical response of nanoscale alloys; the study is restricted to nanoscale samples where defect nucleation is suppressed, so the phenomenon cannot be observed in bulk samples due to premature dislocation generation.. Future work: Future work should prioritize integrating capabilities of 0.1 nm precision in displacement loading and nano-newton level force measurement accuracy into in situ TEM mechanical stages to obtain tensile curves.. Quote: "Under tensile loading, the HEA lattices are observed to undergo a sudden loss of ordering as the elastic strain reached ∽ 10%."

card: Paper card. Question: Does extreme plastic deformation induce solid-state amorphization in the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, and what are the mechanisms and mechanical implications of this transformation?. System: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi (Cantor) high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting and spray forming followed by swaging to a cold work strain of ~80% (nominal strain 0.8); subsequent testing via quasi-static uniaxial compression (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹), dynamic uniaxial compression (strain rate 1.7 × 10³ s⁻¹), and dynamic shear using forced hat-shaped geometry (shear strain rate 6 × 10⁵ s⁻¹, local strain >1.5). Test conditions: Quasi-static compression at room temperature; dynamic compression and shear at initial temperature of 77 K; strain rates ranging from 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 6 × 10⁵ s⁻¹; strains up to 1.5. Findings: Amorphous islands of roughly 10 nm size and amorphous bands were observed in highly deformed regions, confirmed by high-resolution TEM and Fourier-transformed diffractographs showing diffuse scattering.; The alloy exhibited high strength between 1 and 2 GPa across all strain rates, with quasi-static work hardening continuing up to a strain of 0.8 despite pre-deformation.; In dynamic shear experiments, the equivalent strain reached 1.5, significantly higher than in quasi-static tests, leading to adiabatic shear localization.; The volume fraction of amorphous material scales with the intersections of deformation bands containing stacking faults, twins, and hcp ε-martensite.; The absorbed deviatoric strain energy (area under shear stress-strain curves) for predeformed materials was approximately 3200 MPa, roughly twice that of the fully annealed alloy (~1600 MPa).; No apparent chemical segregation was found in the vicinity of amorphous materials, suggesting the amorphization is deformation-induced rather than a preparation artifact.; The critical dislocation density for the fcc→hcp transformation was predicted to be ρ ~ 8 × 10¹⁵ m⁻² based on a stacking-fault energy of ~20 mJ m⁻².. Mechanism: The authors propose that coordinated propagation of stacking faults and twins along {111} planes generates high-deformation regions that reorganize into hexagonal packets; when the defect density reaches a critical level, the free energy of the heavily deformed fcc/hcp structures becomes comparable to that of the amorphous phase, triggering a solid-state transformation to amorphous material at the intersections of these deformation bands.. Limitations: The authors state that determining the precise parameters for the sigmoidal relationship between amorphous volume fraction and plastic strain requires significant and systematic efforts using displacement-controlled experiments, which is nontrivial for dynamic testing.. Future work: The authors propose tailoring the composition to further lower the stacking-fault energy and optimizing thermal-mechanical treatment to introduce higher defect densities to maximize beneficial effects for creating new alloys designed for extreme loading environments.. Quote: "When the defect density in these regions reaches a critical level, they generate islands of amorphous material."

card: Paper card. Question: How does plastic deformation at the crack tip of an ultrafine-grained CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy lead to a crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation, and what are the resulting toughening mechanisms?. System: CrMnFeCoNi Cantor high-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition) in ultrafine-grained (UFG, ~500 nm) and coarse-grained (CG, ~10 μm) states. Processing: UFG: Arc-melted ingots solution-treated at 1100°C for 2 hours, hot forged at 1000°C, cold rolled to 1 mm, then annealed at 650°C for 30 min; CG: Arc-melted ingots solution-treated at 1473 K for 48 hours, cold rolled to 2 mm, then annealed at 850°C for 2 hours; samples thinned to ~100 μm and twin jet polished at ~−30°C with 20.5 V. Test conditions: In situ TEM tensile straining at room temperature using Gatan cooling strain holder; strain rate ~1 × 10−4/s; electron beam voltages of 300 kV (JEM 3000F) and 200 kV (JEM 2200FS); MD simulations at 5 K with strain rate 1 × 108/s. Findings: The crack-tip structural evolution follows a sequence: crystalline → lamellar → spotted → amorphous patterns.; Lamellar areas contain alternate crystalline and amorphous bands with average thicknesses of ~1.7 nm and ~2.3 nm, respectively.; Spotted areas have a higher volume fraction of amorphous phase than crystalline phase, with crystalline regions comprising less than 10%.; Mean dislocation density in spotted areas of UFG samples is 5.6 × 10^17/m², nearly one order of magnitude higher than the 7.6 × 10^16/m² in CG samples.; Amorphous nanobridges formed in the crack wake of UFG samples have widths less than 100 nm and exhibit ductile deformation before failure.; Electron beam illumination causes recrystallization of amorphous nanobridges, whereas storage at room temperature for 3 months maintains the amorphous structure.; No appreciable compositional variations were observed in amorphous, spotted, or lamellar areas; elemental distributions remain nearly equiatomic.. Mechanism: Solid-state amorphization stems from high lattice friction and high grain boundary resistance to dislocation glide in ultrafine-grained microstructures, which promote the buildup of high dislocation densities (critical density ~5.6 × 10^17/m²) and high stresses at the crack tip, triggering the transformation.. Limitations: The study notes that high-quality five-element interatomic potentials for HEAs are still under development, necessitating the use of a binary Cu-Al model for MD simulations; the effect of low-angle vs. high-angle grain boundaries could not be compared due to the low fraction of low-angle boundaries (~2%); and the quantitative evaluation of fracture toughness enhancement requires direct experimental measurements.. Future work: The authors state that the toughening effects need to be quantitatively evaluated by direct experimental measurements of fracture toughness in the future, and that the mechanism warrants further study when high-quality interatomic potentials for the Cantor alloy become available.. Quote: "We find that the crack-tip structural evolution involves a sequence of formation of the crystalline, lamellar, spotted, and amorphous patterns"

card: Paper card. Question: How can elemental partitioning-mediated crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation be realized under quasi-static deformation to achieve ultrahigh strength and large plasticity in a crystal-glass nanolaminated composite?. System: Cr-Ni-Co (crystalline)/Zr-Ti-Nb-Hf-Ni-Co (amorphous) nanolaminated composite; specific compositions: Cr35Ni33Co32 (at.%) and Zr28Ti24Nb22Hf19Ni6Co1 (at.%). Processing: Magnetron sputtering with alternate deposition of CrCoNi and TiZrNbHf targets; substrate temperature below 50 °C; Ar working pressure 4 × 10−3 mbar; deposition rates 3 nm/min (CrCoNi) and 5 nm/min (TiZrNbHf); layer thicknesses 17.0 nm (crystalline) and 6.7 nm (amorphous). Test conditions: Quasi-static pillar compression at strain rates of ~2 × 10−3 s−1; in-situ TEM cyclic loading-unloading compression; micro-indentation for ex-situ TEM and APT analysis. Findings: The crystal-glass nanolaminated alloy exhibits a yield strength of 3.7 GPa and homogeneous plastic deformation of ~20% strain in compression.; The crystalline Cr-Ni-Co phase transforms into an amorphous phase upon plastic deformation, confirmed by a drastic reduction in crystalline diffraction spots and the appearance of an amorphous halo ring in SAED.; Elemental partitioning occurs during deformation, with Ni, Co, and Cr contents in the original Zr-rich region increasing from 6 at.%, 1 at.%, 0 at.% to 35 at.%, 25 at.%, 20 at.%.; The radius of the amorphous halo ring in SAED increases after deformation, indicating a change in short-range-order (SRO) structure towards the atomic packing of the Cr, Ni, Co-enriched phase.; The amorphous nanodomains formed have a size below 10 nm, which promotes homogeneous plastic flow and prevents shear band formation.; The material shows strain hardening up to ~22% true strain, contrasting with the strain softening or shear banding observed in reference crystalline and amorphous alloys.. Mechanism: The authors propose that extensive rearrangement of atoms at the crystal-glass interfaces during deformation facilitates elemental partitioning due to the large negative mixing enthalpy among constituent elements. This intermixing transforms the original crystalline phase into an amorphous phase (CA-TRIP). The dislocations emitted from the interface are absorbed by the amorphous phase, and the massive atomic rearrangement induces this phase transformation. The resulting nanodomained amorphous structure with different compositions impedes shear band propagation, enabling global strain hardening and homogeneous plastic flow.. Limitations: The deviation of stress-strain curves after ~20% strain originates from mechanical instability of the pillar sample during inhomogeneous deformation. The study notes that the CA-TRIP phenomenon does not appear in CuZr/Cu systems due to reduced negative mixing enthalpy from high Cu content.. Future work: The authors suggest this enthalpy-guided alloy design strategy provides guidelines for developing dual-phase alloys and may find applications in load-bearing micro-electro-mechanical systems and protective surface coatings.. Quote: "Upon plastic deformation, atomic intermixing occurs between adjacent amorphous and crystalline phases due to extensive rearrangement of atoms at the interfaces."

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the plastic response, dislocation mobility, and defect evolution during nanoindentation in the bcc HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy compared to a random alloy and an elementary Ta crystal?. System: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (Senkov alloy) in random and short-range-ordered (SRO) states; pure Ta crystal. Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS; SRO created via Monte Carlo simulation at 100 K (4.7×10^6 steps); nanoindentation with a repulsive sphere (R=10 nm) at 20 m/s to 4 nm depth, held for 100 ps, then retracted at 20 m/s; temperature maintained at 10 mK. Test conditions: Constant time step of 1 fs; bottom and lateral sides fixed; thermostat at 10 mK; indenter stiffness k=3.3 eV/Å^3; final depth d=4 nm reached at t=200 ps. Findings: The SRO alloy is 10% harder than the random HEA (H_ind increased by 10%).; The SRO alloy exhibits the highest dislocation density, remaining constant at 1.6–1.8×10^16 m^-2 throughout all phases.; The plastic zone in the SRO alloy extends farthest, with 78% of dislocations surviving retraction compared to negligible survival in Ta.; Elemental Ta shows abundant prismatic dislocation loop emission via the lasso mechanism, which is suppressed in both alloys.; The SRO alloy features zero twinning volume, whereas Ta and the random HEA show significant twinning that partially survives retraction.; The reduction in hold hardness is least for the SRO alloy (20%) compared to the elementary crystal (27%), indicating enhanced difficulty of stress relaxation.; Dislocation segment length is shortest in SRO (4.1 nm) compared to random HEA (4.7 nm) and Ta (5.8 nm).. Mechanism: The slow dislocation migration in these alloys, caused by lattice distortion and the presence of B2-ordered precipitates in the SRO state, impedes dislocation motion, prevents the formation of extended semiloops required for the lasso mechanism, and thwarts the coordinated crystal rotations necessary for twinning.. Limitations: The study uses ideal defect-free crystals with negligible initial dislocation density; the simulation temperature of 10 mK minimizes thermal vibrations but may not reflect behavior at higher temperatures where dislocation avalanches occur; the phase transformation in the SRO sample disappears after unloading, making quantification difficult.. Future work: The authors suggest that the absence of twinning in the SRO alloy might change for an alloy with larger B2 precipitates.. Quote: "Short-range order—besides making the alloy both stiffer and harder—further increases the size of the plastic zone and the dislocation density there."

Paper card. Question: How does short-range order (SRO) and the resulting B2 precipitates affect the mechanical properties, dislocation dynamics, and phase stability of a bcc HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy during nanoindentation compared to a random alloy and pure Ta?. System: HfNbTaTiZr (bcc high-entropy alloy) with and without short-range order; pure Ta crystal. Processing: Monte Carlo procedure to introduce short-range order; Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with a volume > 20 million atoms; Nanoindentation simulation. Test conditions: Nanoindentation loading and unloading cycles; Pressure range under indenter; Comparison of random vs. SRO alloy vs. pure Ta. Findings: Short-range order causes a slight stiffening of elastic constants and an increase in indentation hardness on the 10% level.; Dislocation emission from the plastic zone is strongly impeded or absent in the alloys compared to pure Ta.; Dislocation recovery after indenter withdrawal is constrained: the plastic zone radius shrinks by 50% in pure Ta, 30% in the random alloy, and stays approximately constant in the SRO alloy.; Dislocation densities in the plastic zone are highest for the alloys, particularly the SRO alloy.; Twinning is strongest in the random alloy but shrinks to one third of its volume after unloading.; No twinning is found in the SRO alloy; instead, a limited transition to the hcp phase occurs next to the indenter.; HfTi-rich precipitates in the B2 structure impede dislocation motion and contribute to hardening.. Mechanism: The generation of HfTi-rich precipitates in the B2 structure impedes dislocation motion and helps hardening. The breaking of crystal symmetry and presence of B2 precipitates in the SRO alloy prevent the coordinated motion necessary for twin formation, favoring a limited transition to the hcp phase. Dislocation mobility is decreased in the alloys, leading to constrained recovery and higher dislocation densities.. Limitations: The text notes that distinguishing a distorted omega phase from a distorted bcc phase is difficult, and that Common Neighbor Analysis (CNA) can misidentify phases under inhomogeneous strain.. Future work: Detailed understanding of plasticity might allow design of future alloys with improved performance.. Quote: "Short-range order was introduced into the sample by a Monte Carlo procedure."

W2758161787.title: Atomistic Studies of Nanoindentation—A Review of Recent Advances

card: Paper card. Question: Which powder metallurgy processing route (CIP+sintering, HIP, swaging, or SPS) combined with subsequent deformation (HPT) yields a fully dense, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy with refined microstructure and acceptable mechanical properties?. System: HfNbTaTiZr equiatomic high entropy alloy. Processing: Three initial powder types were used: (1) Elemental powders mixed for 10 h at 45 rpm, cold isostatically pressed (CIP) at 400 MPa, then sintered at 1400 °C for 16 h; (2) Mechanically alloyed (MA) powders milled for 42 h; (3) Gas atomized (AT) powders. Sintering was performed at 1400 °C for 16 h in vacuum. Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) was at 1400 °C for 2 h under 190 MPa. Swaging was at 950 °C with an envelope of beta-titanium alloy. Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) was at 1300 °C for 2 min under 80 MPa. High Pressure Torsion (HPT) was at room temperature with 2.5 GPa pressure and 15 revolutions.. Test conditions: Vickers hardness measured with 98.1 N load (ISO 6507); microstructure analyzed via LM, SEM (BSE mode), and XRD (Cu Kα); oxygen content measured by gas fusion; porosity determined by image analysis; positron lifetime spectroscopy used for defect characterization.. Findings: Swaging of sintered specimens resulted in cracking and failure, preventing full densification.; SPS of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders produced a fully dense but brittle specimen with high oxygen content (~1.07 wt %).; SPS of gas atomized (AT) powder with low oxygen content (~0.12 wt %) resulted in a fully dense, single-phase bcc specimen.; High pressure torsion (HPT) of the AT-SPS specimen refined the grain size from ~50 μm to below 500 nm (0.5 μm).; The AT-SPS-HPT specimen achieved a hardness of 410 HV10 (Abstract) and 584 HV10 (Section 4.3), attributed to grain refinement and dislocation density exceeding 5 × 10^14 m^-2.; Samples processed via CIP followed by HIP exhibited significantly lower hardness (~150 HV10) due to incomplete dissolution of elements and lack of a single-phase random solid solution.; Oxygen content above 0.8 wt % caused a sharp increase in hardness due to the formation of HfO2 particles.. Mechanism: The authors argue that oxygen contamination is the primary cause of embrittlement and prevents the formation of a single-phase random solid solution. The high oxygen content in MA powders leads to the formation of stable HfO2 oxides which cause brittleness. The single-phase bcc structure in the AT-SPS sample is attributed to the high cooling rate (~300 °C/min) during SPS, which suppresses the formation of secondary phases (bcc2 and hcp). Grain refinement and increased hardness in HPT-processed samples are caused by the formation of a high density of dislocations (>5 × 10^14 m^-2) and the presence of oxide particles in oxygen-rich samples.. Limitations: Swaging caused specimen cracking due to brittleness likely induced by high oxygen content (~0.75 wt %) or inappropriate deformation temperature/strain rate. The MA-SPS-HPT specimen broke into pieces during HPT, making its results disputable. Samples prepared by CIP and HIP retained considerable porosity and chemical inhomogeneities. The low hardness of HEAP-HIP samples could not be fully explained, though porosity and phase composition were suspected factors.. Future work: The authors state that the possibility of hot deformation of the alloy with increased oxygen content cannot be excluded under suitable conditions (i.e., low strain rate, or higher processing temperature), but this possibility needs more detailed study.. Quote: "The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the proportions of high-density elements Hf and Ta affect the mechanical properties (strength, elastic modulus, dislocation density) of Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloys, and can a low-density composition be successfully formed via laser melting deposition (LMD) to overcome microstructural coarsening?. System: Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloys, specifically HfxNbTaxTiZr (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) and the designed low-density Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with NPT system relaxation and strain rate of 4 × 10^8 s^-1; Experimental preparation via arc melting for as-cast samples and Laser Melting Deposition (LMD) using a 3 kW semiconductor laser (wavelength 900–1070 nm), laser power 600–1400 W, scanning rate 4 mm/s, powder feeding rate 8 g/min, and height increment 0.5 mm. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a constant displacement speed of 0.3 mm/min; XRD analysis (10~90° 2θ, 10°/min); SEM and EBSD for microstructure; Vickers hardness testing. Findings: MD simulations show that decreasing the Ta element proportion reduces the yield strength of the HEA.; Decreasing the Hf element proportion increases the yield strength of the HEA.; Simultaneously decreasing Hf and Ta ratios reduces the elastic modulus and strength, leading to microstructure coarsening in as-cast samples.; LMD processing refines the grain size of Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr from 300 μm (as-cast) to 20–80 μm (as-deposited).; The as-deposited Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr HEA exhibits a yield strength (σs) of 925 ± 9 MPa, compared to 730 ± 23 MPa for the as-cast version.; The as-deposited low-density alloy achieves strength similar to the as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA (σs = 970 ± 15 MPa).; The as-deposited microstructure shows an alternating distribution of coarse columnar grains and fine equiaxed grains along the z-direction.; Dislocation density in the as-deposited alloy is higher than in as-cast samples due to thermal stress accumulation during LMD.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength increase in as-deposited samples to grain refinement and the Hall-Petch relation, where grain boundaries resist slip transfer. The coarsening in as-cast low-Hf/Ta alloys is explained by the reduction in these elements. The formation of columnar grains in LMD is caused by epitaxial growth from successive thermal cycles, while equiaxed grains form due to lower nucleation barriers, reducing anisotropy. Increased mechanical properties in LMD samples are also linked to the accumulation of thermal stress increasing dislocation density.. Limitations: The MD simulation model scale is too small to accurately reflect the effect of grain boundaries and grain size on alloy properties, leading to quantitative differences between simulated and actual values.. Future work: The authors suggest that while MD simulation has quantitative limitations, its qualitative analysis reduces the amount of experiments needed in component design, and combining it with additive manufacturing technology has good application prospects for engineering.. Quote: "The simultaneous decrease in the ratio of Hf and Ta elements reduces the elastic modulus and strength of HEA and leads to the coarsening of the alloy microstructure."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the indentation hardness of single-phase fcc FexNi1-x alloys vary with stoichiometry, and what microphysical mechanisms (specifically stacking fault energies and dislocation behavior) govern this variation?. System: Single-phase fcc FexNi1-x solid solutions (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) compared to elemental fcc-Fe and fcc-Ni. Processing: Molecular dynamics simulation using the Bonny et al. potential; crystals created with random Fe/Ni placement on fcc lattice sites (66.4 nm lateral, 50.3 nm depth, ~20.8 million atoms); relaxed in NPT ensemble to ~1 mK; nanoindentation performed with a repulsive spherical indenter (R=10 nm, k=10 eV/Å3) moving at 20 m/s to a depth of 4 nm over 200 ps, held for 100 ps, then retracted at 20 m/s. Test conditions: Temperature: ~1 mK (to minimize thermal vibrations); Indenter velocity: 20 m/s; Final indentation depth: 4 nm; Time step: 1 fs; LAMMPS code with OVITO for analysis. Findings: Indentation hardness is maximum for the equiatomic alloy (x=0.5), agreeing with experimental uniaxial strain results.; The unstable stacking fault energy (USFE) exhibits a maximum at intermediate stoichiometries (x=0.5), correlating directly with the hardness maximum.; Loop emission from the plastic zone becomes less pronounced with increasing Fe content; for pure fcc-Fe, only a single loop is ejected.; The total length of the dislocation network and the number of atoms in stacking faults within the plastic zone increase continuously with Fe content.; The volume of twinned regions is highest for elemental solids and decreases for the alloys due to inefficient concerted dislocation motion in concentrated compositions.; The fraction of screw dislocation segments in the plastic zone increases with Fe content, reaching high values in Fe-rich samples.; Surface imprints show increasing pile-up heights with increasing Fe content, with pure Fe exhibiting the highest hillocks.; The fraction of sessile dislocations (stair-rod, Hirth, Frank partials) reaches almost 20% for the equiatomic Fe50Ni50 alloy after tip retraction.. Mechanism: The authors explain the hardness maximum at x=0.5 by the increase in unstable stacking fault energy (USFE), which quantifies the energy barrier for stacking fault creation and dislocation glide. The reduced loop emission and larger plastic zone in Fe-rich alloys are attributed to the difficulty of dislocation cross-slip required for loop formation. The suppression of twinning in alloys is explained by local compositional fluctuations reducing the probability of the concerted motion of dislocations on adjacent parallel lattice planes required for twin growth.. Limitations: The authors note that small quantitative differences in indentation results are expected between the 1-mK simulation and room temperature experiments, though plasticity mechanisms remain unchanged. They also mention that previous studies using the Choi potential were not well-suited for this subsystem because it yielded negative SFE for pure Fe and monotonic USFE decrease.. Future work: The authors propose that the findings could be used for hardness engineering by creating gradient profiles in stoichiometry via ion implantation or plasma deposition to generate hardness profiles. They suggest experimental verification of the predicted extended dislocation semiloops and larger plastic zones in nano-pillars cut from single-phase FexNi1-x alloys or large single-crystalline grains.. Quote: "The indentation hardness is maximum for the equiatomic alloy, x=0.5."

card: Paper card. Question: How do temperature, strain rate, and grain size influence the micromechanical behavior, phase transformation, and deformation mechanisms of the Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 high-entropy alloy?. System: Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) high-entropy alloy. Processing: Molecular dynamics simulation using LAMMPS with EAM potential functions; model size 30a × 30a × 30a (54,000 atoms); relaxed 50fs under NPT; tensile strain of 0.35 along Y direction at temperatures of 77, 300, 700, and 1000 K and strain rates of 1 × 10^9, 5 × 10^9, 1 × 10^10, 3 × 10^10, and 5 × 10^10 s^-1 under NVT ensemble; grain size variation via Voronoi structure method (10 × 10 × 10 nm^3 models with 2, 4, 6, and 8 grains).. Test conditions: Temperatures: 77 K, 300 K, 700 K, 1000 K; Strain rates: 1 × 10^9 s^-1 to 5 × 10^10 s^-1; Strain: up to 0.35; Grain sizes: varied by number of grains (2, 4, 6, 8) in 10 nm^3 models.. Findings: The alloy undergoes a phase transition from BCC to FCC during tensile loading, with FCC reaching a maximum content of about 51% at 0.2 strain.; At high temperatures (e.g., 1000 K) and low strain rates (1 × 10^9 s^-1), grain boundary slip is the dominant deformation mechanism.; At low temperatures (e.g., 77 K) and high strain rates (1 × 10^10 s^-1), dislocation slip replaces grain boundary slip as the dominant mechanism.; Dislocation density at 77 K was 4.6 × 10^17 m^-2 (1 × 10^9 s^-1) and 5 × 10^17 m^-2 (1 × 10^10 s^-1), while at 1000 K it was 2.5 × 10^16 m^-2 and 1 × 10^17 m^-2 respectively.; The elastic modulus at 300 K and 1 × 10^10 s^-1 was calculated as 116.7 GPa.; Ultimate strength increases with increasing strain rate, showing a positive correlation.; An inverse Hall–Petch relationship was observed where strength decreased when grain size became too small (e.g., 6 and 8 grains had lower strength than 4 grains).; The alloy exhibits a transition from single crystal to polycrystal during the tensile process.. Mechanism: At high temperatures, intensified thermal motion causes atoms at grain boundaries to break away and become disordered, leading to grain boundary slip. At low temperatures and high strain rates, dislocations are generated within grains, slip, and accumulate at boundaries to form knots, increasing resistance to deformation. The inverse Hall–Petch effect occurs because small grain sizes hinder dislocation movement and entanglement within grains and make grain boundaries more prone to breakdown.. Limitations: The study is based on molecular dynamics simulations which may not fully capture all experimental conditions; the specific potential function used was fitted by Zhou et al. and verified against limited experimental data.. Future work: The study offers a new compositional window for additive manufactured lightweight high-strength materials and provides theoretical guidance for improving service performance and structural regulation of HEAs.. Quote: "The Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 alloy changes from a single crystal to a polycrystal during the tensile process, and the transition of the Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) high-entropy alloy from the BCC phase to the FCC phase occurs."

W2792744269.title: Transformation induced softening and plasticity in high entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How can a precipitation-strengthening strategy be used to design a high-entropy/medium-entropy alloy that sustains ultrahigh strength and excellent ductility simultaneously across a wide temperature range from cryogenic to elevated temperatures?. System: Al5(CoNiV)95 (at %) alloy, a CoNiV-based face-centered cubic (fcc)/B2 duplex medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with 5 at% Al added to an equiatomic fcc-structured CoNiV matrix; also Al7(CoNiV)93 for comparison. Processing: Arc-melting high-purity (>99.9 at%) Al, Co, Ni, and V metals followed by suction-casting into a Cu mold; homogenization at 1373 K for 8 hours with water quenching; cold rolling with 65% thickness reduction; annealing at 1173 K for 1 hour with water quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 77 K, 298 K, 723 K, and 1073 K using a universal testing machine at a fixed strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; microstructural analysis via XRD, EBSD, TEM, and synchrotron high-energy XRD on tensile-fractured samples. Findings: At room temperature (298 K), the alloy exhibited a yield strength of 1.1 GPa, ultimate tensile strength of 1.5 GPa, and tensile elongation of ~34%.; At cryogenic temperature (77 K), yield strength increased to 1.4 GPa, ultimate tensile strength to 1.9 GPa, with fracture elongation of ~38%.; At intermediate temperature (723 K), the alloy maintained a yield strength of 1.1 GPa with serrated stress-strain response and high strain hardening rates.; At high temperature (1073 K), the alloy showed enhanced ductility of ~74% and ultimate tensile strength of 0.28 GPa, attributed to dynamic recrystallization.; The alloy achieved the highest specific yield strength among reported ductile HEAs at ~150.2 MPa·cm³/g.; The volume fraction of the B2 phase in Al5(CoNiV)95 was estimated at ~6%, with B2 grain sizes ranging from several hundred nanometers to ~1 μm.; In the Al7(CoNiV)93 variant, increasing Al content raised the B2 phase volume fraction to ~21% and resulted in ~280% superplastic elongation at 1073 K.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength-ductility synergy to multiple deformation mechanisms: precipitation strengthening from Al-rich B2 nanoparticles; dynamic Hall-Petch effect where twin boundaries reduce dislocation mean free path; twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) triggered by low stacking fault energy (SFE) in the fcc matrix; dynamic strain aging (DSA) at 723 K causing flow serrations; and dynamic recrystallization (DRX) enabling superplasticity at 1073 K. The B2 precipitates constrain the soft fcc matrix, generating back stresses, while twins mitigate interfacial stress concentrations to delay fracture.. Limitations: The authors note that the Al7(CoNiV)93 variant exhibited a ductile-brittle transition when lowering temperature from 298 to 77 K due to increased B2 precipitate density. Additionally, the superplastic elongation of the Al5(CoNiV)95 alloy (~74%) was insufficient compared to other microduplex alloys, attributed to deformation-enhanced grain growth which could be mitigated by using high strain rates.. Future work: The authors suggest that high strain rates could be used to overcome deformation-enhanced grain growth and improve superplastic elongation. They also propose that the design strategy can be adapted by adjusting Al content to optimize the balance between strength and ductility, and that combining chemical complexity with conventional strengthening principles can justify the industrial costs of M/HEAs.. Quote: "The ability of the alloy presented here to sustain this excellent strength-ductility synergy over a wide temperature range is aided by multiple deformation mechanisms i.e., twins, stacking faults, dynamic strain aging, and dynamic recrystallization."

card: Paper card. Question: Whether the deformation of pure molybdenum, a refractory metal with no known polymorphs, can ever be coupled with a structural transformation that leads to the emergence of new metastable crystalline lattices under high-stress conditions.. System: Pure molybdenum (Mo) film (99.9 wt.% pure). Processing: In situ tensile testing inside a transmission electron microscope (TEM) at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder; loading controlled by intermittent displacement with a time resolution of 0.1 s; crack tip configuration {010}<001>.. Test conditions: Room temperature; local shear stress ~8 GPa; local tensile stresses ~20.7±2.6 GPa along [100] and ~5.6±2.3 GPa along [010]; strain rate in MD simulations 10^7 s^-1 at 300 K.. Findings: A structural transformation from <001>-oriented body-centred cubic (bcc1) to <110>-oriented face-centred cubic (fcc) was observed at crack tips.; The fcc domains subsequently reverted to <111>-oriented body-centred cubic domains (bcc2), equivalent to a lattice rotation of 54.7°.; Approximately 15.4% tensile strain was accommodated through the bcc1→fcc→bcc2 sequence.; The fcc structure was identified as a well-defined metastable state with a lattice parameter a=0.409 nm.; The orientation relationship between bcc1 and fcc follows the Nishiyama–Wassermann (N–W) relationship: (110)bcc1//(111)fcc and [001]bcc1//[10-1]fcc.; The orientation relationship between fcc and bcc2 follows the Kurdjumov–Sachs (K–S) relationship: (1-11)fcc//(011)bcc2 and [10-1]fcc//[1-11]bcc2.; Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed the atomic shear mechanism along <110> for bcc1→fcc and along {111}fcc for fcc→bcc2.; Twinning was suppressed in the {010}<001> crack configuration, whereas twinning was activated in {001}<110> configurations.. Mechanism: The authors argue that when the easy deformation path (dislocation slip and twinning) is suppressed or bypassed, extremely high shear stresses (>7 GPa) thermodynamically drive the energetically uphill bcc-to-fcc transition to release local stress concentration. The fcc phase acts as a metastable intermediate state bridging two bcc orientations via N–W and K–S crystallographic relationships, allowing for massive shear deformation and lattice rotation without conventional twinning.. Limitations: The intermediate fcc phase is difficult to detect in bulk samples or uniaxial tests because the transformation progresses rapidly to the final bcc state without confinement; the phase is only observable in localized, well-confined deformation areas like crack tips in nanometer-scaled samples.. Future work: The authors suggest that phase transformations coupled with large shear deformation or catastrophic yielding may occur in high-stress deformation conditions for other elemental metals without polymorphs, implying the mechanism is important for nanomaterials deformed under high-stress conditions.. Quote: "Plastic deformation via structural transitions has never been reported for pure molybdenum, while transformation coupled with plasticity is well known for many alloys and ceramics."

W3128316150.title: Evidence of FCC to HCP and BCC-martensitic transformations in a CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy by severe plastic deformation

card: Paper card. Question: How do crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC), temperature, and alloying elements influence the dry sliding wear rate, hardness, and coefficient of friction of high-entropy alloys?. System: Ingot cast high-entropy alloys including the Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi) and its variations (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiTiAl, CoCrFeNiCu, CoCrFeNiS), categorized by FCC, BCC, and dual-phase (FCC+BCC) crystal structures.. Processing: Manufacturing methods include arc melting (most common), vacuum arc melting, induction melting, and spark plasma sintering (SPS); ingots are remelted multiple times for homogeneity, and composites are prepared by mixing powders (e.g., with MoS2, graphite, Ag) before sintering.. Test conditions: Dry sliding conditions using ball-on-disk, pin-on-disk, and ball-on-block setups; counter bodies include Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15); tests conducted at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 600°C and beyond); loads and sliding velocities varied (e.g., 5 N, 0.28 m/s).. Findings: HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC+BCC alloys due to reduced ductility and limited slip systems.; The addition of Al and Ti to the Cantor alloy increased hardness by up to 40% and promoted a transition from FCC to harder BCC phases.; Wear rates for most HEAs decreased after reaching a certain elevated temperature due to the formation of a protective oxide layer at the sliding interface.; The addition of 0.2 to 1 at.% Cu to CoCrFeNi HEA reduced the wear rate at 600°C by 40–45% due to the lubricating nature of Cu at high temperatures.; Self-lubricating composites with MoS2 and graphite showed significantly lower coefficients of friction but higher wear rates above 200°C compared to the base SPSed HEA.; FCC phase HEAs exhibited higher coefficients of friction and lower hardness compared to BCC phase HEAs, resulting in larger wear tracks.; The addition of V increased hardness but subsequently increased the wear rate after a certain percentage was added.. Mechanism: The superior wear resistance of BCC phases is attributed to limited slip systems causing strong but brittle behavior. At elevated temperatures, wear reduction is driven by the formation of a protective oxide layer (tribo-oxidation) or self-lubricating phases (e.g., CrxSy, sheared Cu) that reduce friction and protect the surface. The 'cocktail effect' and lattice distortion contribute to solid solution strengthening and high hardness.. Limitations: The review notes that intrinsic brittleness in BCC alloys is a trade-off for wear resistance. The oxidation mechanisms are complex due to multiple elements, and the influence of individual elements can taper off or become ill-advised at certain ratios (e.g., excessive brittleness from C or Cr3C2). Manufacturing homogeneity is challenging due to varying densities and melting points.. Future work: Future studies should focus on understanding tribo-oxidation behavior in different environmental conditions, creating guidelines for selecting solid lubricants, exploring additive manufacturing techniques (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) for HEA composites, and conducting detailed cost-performance matrix studies against conventional alloys.. Quote: "In general, HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC + BCC alloys."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the high-temperature tensile mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 refractory high-entropy alloy, and can a constitutive model predict its flow behavior?. System: NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 (Refractory High-Entropy Alloy). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (5–8 remelts), drop-casting into water-cooled copper mold, cold rolling (50% thickness reduction), stress-relief annealing (800 °C, 10 min), and water quenching.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 298–1027 K (up to 1273 K mentioned in abstract) with strain rates of 0.001–0.1 s⁻¹; infrared heating with 5 min hold; samples coated with boron nitride paint.. Findings: At 473 K, the alloy exhibited a tensile ductility of 12%.; In the 673–873 K range, yield strength remained above 800 MPa while ductility was reduced.; A 'high-temperature plateau' in strength was observed between 873 K and 1073 K where strength changes were negligible.; At 1223 K, plasticity rose to more than 30% while yield strength decreased significantly.; Nanoindentation revealed a uniform nanohardness of 5.13 ± 0.01 GPa across dendritic and interdendritic regions.; Deformation was controlled by dislocation slip with no evidence of deformation twins.; The deformation activation energy (Q) was calculated to be 379 kJ/mol.; The hyperbolic sine constitutive model predicted peak stress with a maximum error of about 100 MPa.. Mechanism: Plastic deformation is controlled by dislocation slip, where the morphology and density of dislocations dictate mechanical properties. The high-temperature strength plateau is attributed to a competition between work hardening (dislocation accumulation) and softening mechanisms (dynamic recovery or recrystallization), while the unusual strength retention is speculated to involve edge dislocations acting as barriers via thermal super-jogging.. Limitations: The study notes that the mechanism for the retained strength at high temperatures is currently unknown and that the observed low-plasticity plateau between 873 K and 1073 K contradicts general alloy experience; potential causes like dynamic oxygen embrittlement or nanoscale precipitation were considered but not fully confirmed.. Future work: The authors propose that the potential nanoscale precipitates responsible for ductility loss at 1073 K, which were too small to be seen in TEM, will be the subject of another study.. Quote: "At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys."

card: Paper card. Question: What alloying and scaling conditions lead to the strongest both ductile and stable materials?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) thin films and pillars. Processing: d.c. magnetron co-sputtering on (100) silicon or sapphire substrates at room temperature; Ion beam-assisted deposition (IBAD) used with 1.2 keV beam energy, 5 mA current, and 35° incidence angle to reduce grain size; Focused Ga ion beams (FIB) used to mill pillars with diameters of ~1 μm, 500, 200, and 100 nm. Test conditions: Microcompression tests at a strain rate of 2 × 10−3 s−1; Thermal annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days in argon atmosphere. Findings: HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ~10 GPa, one order of magnitude higher than the bulk form.; Compressive plastic strains over 30% were achieved in smaller pillars without cracking.; 580-nm Normal HEA pillars show a yield strength of ~5 GPa, while 580-nm IBAD HEA pillars reach ~6.5 GPa.; Smallest IBAD HEA pillars (~70–100 nm diameter) exhibit yield strengths of ~8–10 GPa.; After annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days, HEA pillars retain a high yield strength of ~5 GPa, whereas pure W films show significant grain growth and pore formation.; IBAD HEA pillars exhibit a log–log slope of −0.2 for the relationship between flow stress and pillar diameter, indicating the lowest size dependence among reported pillars.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is attributed to the simultaneous operation of four strengthening mechanisms: lattice friction, Taylor hardening, source-controlled strength, and grain-boundary strengthening. The excellent thermal stability is attributed to relatively low grain-boundary energy due to the highly disordered grain interiors in HEAs, which lowers the driving force for grain-boundary migration compared to pure metals.. Limitations: The text notes that large pillars (>1 μm) experience cracking at strains larger than ~20% and that the smallest pillars (~70–100 nm) show higher scattering levels in strength due to inhomogeneous distribution of grain boundaries.. Future work: The authors state that mechanical tests for small-scale HEAs at high temperatures are still needed to prove their capability as high-temperature materials, and that further work is required to optimize small-scale HEAs for applications, such as determining the best alloying elements and optimized grain and specimen size combinations.. Quote: "Here we report a strategy for the fabrication of refractory HEA thin films and small-sized pillars that consist of strongly textured, columnar and nanometre-sized grains."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a hierarchical architecture involving secondary nanoprecipitates form inside primary nanoprecipitates in high-entropy alloys, and can an ultrahigh strength be achieved through a high density of such intragranular hierarchical nanoprecipitates?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (atomic %). Processing: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 49 hours (45h dry + 4h wet with ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1000°C, 30 MPa pressure, 90°C/min heating rate, and <8 Pa vacuum.. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension using in situ SEM microtensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM compression tests at room temperature with an axial displacement rate of 3 nm s–1.. Findings: Tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.; Failure strain of ~5.2% achieved alongside the ultrahigh strength values.; Microstructure consists of a primary fcc phase (~82.3 vol %) and a small amount of bcc phase (~17.7 vol %).; The fcc matrix contains a high density of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates: primary γ′ (L12 structure, ~57 nm avg diameter, ~62 vol % in fcc) and secondary γ* (A1 structure, several nm to tens of nm).; Average spacing between adjacent γ′ nanoprecipitates is ~11 nm.; Dislocations were observed to shear both the primary γ′ and secondary γ* precipitates during in situ TEM compression.; Grain diameters average ~409 nm for the fcc phase and ~227 nm for the bcc phase.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is primarily attributed to precipitation strengthening via the shearing mechanism, where dislocations shear both the primary coherent γ′ precipitates and the secondary coherent γ* precipitates, creating an 'exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect' due to the hierarchical obstacle distribution. Additional contributions come from grain-boundary strengthening (due to submicrometer grains) and load transfer via the hard bcc phase.. Limitations: The chemical composition of the secondary γ* precipitates could not be obtained due to their very small sizes.. Future work: The authors suggest the design strategy provides insight for achieving ultrahigh strength in HEAs or other multicomponent alloys, implying further exploration of hierarchical architectures, though specific future experiments are not explicitly detailed beyond the general validation of the strategy.. Quote: "Here, we report a strategy for the design and fabrication of HEAs that can achieve ultrahigh tensile strengths."
