card: Paper card. Question: What are the unique elastic and plastic deformation mechanisms of a single-phase BCC NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and how do they compare to conventional BCC alloys?. System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 atomic %). Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, sealed in quartz tubes, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.. Test conditions: In situ neutron diffraction compression tests at RT, 500°C, 700°C, and 900°C with strain rate of 1 × 10−4 s−1; Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) from 100 to 650 kHz; First-principles DFT calculations at absolute zero and RT; Machine Learning predictions; HAADF-STEM imaging of 15% deformed samples.. Findings: Yield strength decreased from 1064 MPa at RT to 595 MPa at 900°C.; Work-hardening exponent decreased from 0.2732 at RT to 0.1199 at 900°C.; The alloy exhibits elastically isotropic deformation behavior at RT (Zener anisotropy AZ ≈ 1.2, Universal anisotropy index AU = 0).; Elastic anisotropy gradually increases at elevated temperatures but shows much smaller variation (AZ from 1.2 at RT to 1.6 at 900°C) compared to conventional alloys.; The dominant mobile dislocations during plastic deformation are edge dislocations (<111> {110}), unlike conventional BCC metals where screw dislocations often dominate.; Single-crystal elastic constants calculated via DFT show good agreement with experimental neutron and RUS data, with relative errors of -15.9% (Young's), -16.6% (shear), and -6.0% (bulk) at RT.; The alloy maintains a single BCC solid solution phase with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm up to 900°C.; Pugh ratio (K/G) and Poisson's ratio (ν > 0.26) indicate the material is intrinsically ductile.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the severely distorted lattice in the HEA, caused by the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii, leads to compositional fluctuations that deviate edge dislocation cores from their neutral planes. This creates wavy dislocation lines, which substantially reduces the mobility of edge dislocations, making them the dominant mobile character compared to conventional BCC metals where edge dislocations annihilate easily.. Limitations: The text notes that the validity of theoretical calculation methods for designing elastically isotropic and ductile BCC HEAs was previously lacking experimental validation, though this paper addresses that. It also mentions that the ML model predictions are somewhat unexpected because the Materials Project database contains ordered compounds, not disordered alloys like HEAs, and lattice distortion effects might cause less accurate results.. Future work: The authors state these discoveries may facilitate the development of possible alloy systems for structural material applications and provide a road map toward the discovery and production of newly designed polycrystalline materials.. Quote: "The dominant type of mobile dislocations during plastic deformation could be edge dislocations, which is different from conventional BCC metals."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the microstructure and mechanical behavior of the Al0.35CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy change when processed via additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) compared to its cast and heat-treated state, particularly regarding strain-rate sensitivity?. System: Al0.35CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (nominal composition, cast from 99% purity elements). Processing: Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) using a B8 machine; 15-layer build with 1 mm layer height, 500 rpm spindle rotation, 31.8 mm/min traversing speed, and 27.9 mm/min actuator feed rate; feedstock annealed at 750 °C for 24 h and water-quenched.. Test conditions: Compression testing at quasi-static (0.001 s⁻¹) and intermediate (1 s⁻¹) strain rates in ambient laboratory conditions; specimen dimensions: 4.5 mm height and 4.5 mm diameter.. Findings: The AFSD process reduced grain size significantly, with EBSD revealing reduced grain sizes along bands of aluminum-rich particles at layer interfaces.; The maximum stress of the AFSD material was 1074 MPa at 0.001 s⁻¹, approximately double the feedstock's 576 MPa.; The advancing side (AS) of the deposit contained a fully FCC structure, while the retreating side (RS) exhibited a dual-phase FCC/BCC structure.; Al-rich particles were observed along layer interfaces on the retreating side, with EDS confirming their composition.; The average annealed hardness of the feedstock was ~175 HV, while the AFSD material showed significantly increased hardness at Al-rich locations.; The feedstock material showed positive strain-rate sensitivity, with maximum stress increasing from 575 MPa (0.001 s⁻¹) to 690 MPa (1 s⁻¹).; The AFSD material exhibited apparent strain-rate insensitivity, with maximum stresses of 1074 MPa (0.001 s⁻¹) and 1057 MPa (1 s⁻¹).; The feedstock material showed pronounced softening indicative of resistance to dynamic recrystallization (DRX), whereas the AFSD material showed stage-III and stage-IV hardening characteristic of DRX.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength increase to the Hall–Petch effect from grain refinement and the formation of a split FCC + BCC phase structure. Grain refinement in the AFSD material is attributed to dynamic recrystallization (DRX) and Zener pinning by Al-rich particles at layer interfaces. The resistance to recrystallization in the cast feedstock is attributed to sluggish diffusion behavior.. Limitations: The authors note that the apparent strain-rate insensitivity in the AFSD material may be due to the placement of samples taken from both the advancing and retreating sides of the deposit, which have different local mechanical properties and hardness levels.. Future work: The authors propose that further mechanical performance could be gained from the implementation of a post-deposition heat treatment to dissolve the Al-rich particles and further increase the BCC structure.. Quote: "The overall strength of the deposited material was approximately doubled compared to that of the cast material system with increases in strength at both quasi-static and intermediate strain rates due to the Hall–Petch effect and a split FCC + BCC phase structure."

card: Paper card. Question: How do additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and post-heat treatments influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional casting methods?. System: CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x=0.3, 0.6, 0.85), CoCrFeMnNi, FeCoCrAlCu, Ti25Zr50Nb0Ta25, CoCrFeNiTi, and AA5083/CoCrFeNi composites. Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD/DMD/DLF), and Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM); parameters include layer thickness (20–100 μm), volumetric energy density (VED), laser power (e.g., 400 W), scanning speed (e.g., 1200 mm/s), and pre-heating; post-treatments include High Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1100 °C for 2 h, annealing (750–1000 °C), and solution treatment.. Test conditions: Tensile and compression tests at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K); microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EBSD; wear resistance testing.. Findings: AM-processed HEAs exhibit superior yield strength and ductility compared to casting counterparts due to fine microstructures formed by rapid solidification.; SLM CoCrFeNi specimens showed significantly higher yield strength than arc-melt specimens while retaining significant ductility.; Increasing volumetric energy density (VED) in SLM CoCrFeMnNi reduced holes and cracks, leading to higher ultimate tensile strength.; HIP treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h removed second-phase grain-boundary phases and segregation in Al0.3CoCrFeNi, achieving chemical homogenization.; SEBM AlCoCrFeNi specimens displayed better plasticity than cast specimens due to finer grains and a substantial fraction of ductile FCC phase.; Cryogenic testing (77 K) on LAM-fabricated CrMnFeCoNi HEA enhanced yield strength and ductility, with deformation twinning becoming more obvious at high strain.; Solution treatment of SEBM CoCrFeNiTi HEA improved ductility without lowering strength by removing needle-like Ni3Ti precipitates.; Different AM methods induce substantial differences in yield strength and plasticity; for instance, DLF Al0.3CoCrFeNi showed much lower yield strength compared to SLM and SEBM methods.. Mechanism: The enhanced mechanical properties are primarily ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients and rapid solidification during AM, which leads to fine cellular dendrite structures, high dislocation densities, and suppressed elemental segregation. Post-treatments like HIP and annealing further enhance properties by removing fabrication defects (pores, microcracks) and releasing residual stress, while specific heat treatments can dissolve or modify precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti, B2 phases) to optimize the balance between strength and ductility.. Limitations: Defects such as residual stress, microcracks, and pores exist in as-built AM components, degrading mechanical properties; some AM specimens exhibit anisotropy in mechanical properties due to texture and grain orientation; limited ductility is observed in some Al-rich alloys due to brittle phase appearance; most existing studies focus on tension/compression, with rare data on fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, or corrosion.. Future work: Optimize processing parameters and heat treatment regimes to improve microstructures and reduce residual stress; investigate fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, and corrosion properties; expand research to light-weight and refractory HEAs; develop broader compositional ranges; investigate materials with large differences in melting temperatures; and study effective powder blending methods to reduce agglomeration and increase homogeneity.. Quote: "Compared with the casting counterparts, AM-HEAs were found to have a superior yield strength and ductility as a consequence of the fine microstructure formed during the rapid solidification in the fabrication process."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the high-temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy superalloy (HESA) with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, and how do they compare to conventional superalloys and other HEAs?. System: Ni47.9Al10.2Co16.9Cr7.4Fe8.9Ti5.8Mo0.9Nb1.2W0.4C0.4 (at%) high entropy superalloy (HESA). Processing: Vacuum-arc-melting followed by directional-solidification; solution-heat-treatment at 1210 °C for 10 h; primary aging at 1000 °C for 3 h; secondary aging at 800 °C for 20 h. Test conditions: Tensile tests at strain rate 10^-3 sec^-1 from room temperature to 950 °C; creep tests at 750, 850, and 982 °C under constant stress of 159 MPa. Findings: The HESA possesses a γ matrix and dispersed γ′ precipitates with an average size of 290 nm and 69 vol% after heat treatment.; The γ′ solvus temperature is 1199 °C and the solidus temperature is 1276 °C.; The lattice misfit (δ) between γ and γ′ at 982 °C is calculated to be 0.08%.; The estimated stacking fault energy (SFE) of the HESA matrix is approximately 0.7 J/m², which is lower than that of CMSX-2.; The anti-phase boundary (APB) energy of the γ′ phase in HESA is 0.22 J/m², higher than the 0.19 J/m² in CMSX-2.; The creep rupture life of HESA at 982 °C is about 114 hours, comparable to first-generation Ni-based superalloys like Rene′ 80.; The creep activation energy (Q) for HESA is estimated to be 290 kJ/mol, higher than the 230 kJ/mol for CMSX-2.; At 982 °C, the γ′ precipitates undergo parallel rafting (P-raft) along the stress axis, coarsening from 0.29 μm to 0.5 μm perpendicular and extending to 3 μm parallel to the stress.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the high strength to the high volume fraction of γ′ precipitates, low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, and high anti-phase boundary energy of the precipitates. For creep, the authors argue that the lower SFE and higher activation energy contribute to lower creep rates at intermediate temperatures by making dislocation bowing more difficult. At 982 °C, the positive lattice misfit leads to parallel rafting, which the authors state causes the creep curves to be dominated by tertiary creep behavior, unlike the perpendicular rafting seen in CMSX-2.. Limitations: The authors note that the current γ′ size of 290 nm is smaller than the estimated optimized size of 390 nm for peak strength, suggesting the strength could be increased by 16% with larger precipitates. They also mention that the positive temperature dependence on yield strength is less pronounced compared to CMSX-2.. Future work: The authors propose studying the non-isothermal creep behavior of HESA and suggest that minor additions of γ partitioning elements like Mo and Re could lead to desirable negative lattice misfit for N-type rafting and provide solid-solution strengthening.. Quote: "The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures"

card: Paper card. Question: Can rare-earth-free high magnetic anisotropy be achieved in single-phase high entropy alloy thin films using rapid thermal annealing, and how does the addition of Platinum influence phase ordering and coercivity?. System: FeCoNiMnCu (equiatomic precursor) and (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt (50 at.% Pt addition). Processing: Direct-current magnetron sputtering onto thermally oxidized Si/SiO2 substrates at room temperature or elevated temperatures (20–700 °C), followed by rapid thermal annealing (RTA) at 600 °C for 10–60 seconds in vacuum. Test conditions: Magnetic properties measured via VSM and SQUID; structural analysis via GIXRD, θ-2θ XRD, HAADF-STEM, and SAED; First-Order Reversal Curve (FORC) analysis in in-plane and out-of-plane geometries. Findings: As-grown FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a coercivity of 10 Oe, which increases to 390 Oe after 30 s of RTA at 600 °C (approx. 40-fold increase).; Inclusion of 50 at.% Pt leads to a single L10 high entropy intermetallic phase after 60 s of RTA at 600 °C.; The (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt L10 phase shows a coercivity increase of 3 orders of magnitude, reaching 2.50 kOe (in-plane) and 1.46 kOe (out-of-plane).; The L10 order parameter (S) extracted from XRD intensities is 0.8, indicating significant chemical ordering.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) for FeCoNiMnCu films is 595 ± 45 emu cm−3 (as-grown) and 590 ± 30 emu cm−3 (after RTA).; The effective uniaxial anisotropy constant (Ku) for the Pt-based L10 film is 2 × 10^6 erg cm−3.; RTA induces void formation in 13 nm films after 30 s, covering 45% area fraction, while 50 nm films show <5% area fraction.; DFT calculations suggest Mn-Mn magnetic ordering is ferromagnetic for Mn:Cu ratios ≤ 0.25 and antiferromagnetic for ratios > 0.25.. Mechanism: The authors propose that RTA induces microstructural changes, anisotropic strain, and directional chemical order that strengthen domain wall pinning in FeCoNiMnCu films. For the Pt-containing films, the reduction of cubic symmetry to a tetragonal L10 structure combined with strong spin-orbit coupling from Pt provides the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy, while bimodal coercivity arises from a two-step reversal process involving large (001)-textured grains and smaller randomly oriented grains.. Limitations: The authors note that the extracted Ku is not representative of the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy due to the polycrystalline microstructure and is lower than binary L10 FePt and CoPt alloys. Additionally, the saturation magnetization is reduced compared to bulk FePt and CoPt values.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity could be enhanced through microstructural optimization, specifically by reducing grain size, which may be achieved by adjusting the RTA time and temperature.. Quote: "Inclusion of 50 at.% Pt in the film leads to ordering of a single L10 high entropy intermetallic phase after RTA, along with high magnetic anisotropy and 3 orders of magnitude coercivity increase."

W2026572419.title: Magnetic Materials and Devices for the 21st Century: Stronger, Lighter, and More Energy Efficient

card: Paper card. Question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). Processing: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis. Findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.; Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.; Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.; Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.; The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.; Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.. Mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a high entropy alloy of transition metals absorb significantly higher amounts of hydrogen than its constituent elements, potentially reaching an H/M ratio greater than 2 without using rare-earth elements?. System: Equimolar TiVZrNbHf (High Entropy Alloy). Processing: Arc-melting stoichiometric amounts of Ti, V, Zr, Nb, and Hf (99.6-99.995% purity) five times with re-melting and turning over; sample re-melted with Ti getter to minimize oxygen; hydrogenation performed on ball-milled powder (<50 μm) at 20 bar H2 and 400 °C for 48 h.. Test conditions: Gravimetric measurements at 400 °C; volumetric PCT measurements at 299 °C (±1) with pressure up to ~50 bar and 10 h equilibrium time per point; Thermal Desorption Spectroscopy (TDS) with 5 °C/min heating ramp.. Findings: The as-synthesized TiVZrNbHf alloy crystallizes in a single-phase BCC-type structure with a unit cell parameter a = 3.3659(2) Å.; After hydrogenation at 400 °C for 48 h, the alloy forms a body-centred tetragonal (BCT) lattice with a = 3.2183(4) Å and c = 4.6556(16) Å.; Gravimetric measurements yielded a hydrogen-to-metal ratio (H/M) of 2.42.; Volumetric PCT measurements showed a maximum storage capacity of 2.5 H/M at 53 bar H2, equivalent to 2.7 wt% hydrogen.; Hydrogen desorption occurs in a one-step reaction with onset as low as 200 °C and a maximum pressure peak above 400 °C.; The hydrogen absorption/desorption process is reversible, regaining the BCC-type structure after desorption.; XRD patterns after desorption show doublets indicating phase separation into two different BCC phases with slightly different unit cell parameters.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the large hydrogen storage capacity is due to lattice strain caused by the variation in atomic radii of the constituent elements (δ = 6.82%), which makes it energetically favourable for hydrogen to occupy both tetrahedral and octahedral interstitial sites, a configuration not typically accessible in pure transition metal hydrides.. Limitations: The observed H/M ratio of 2.5 corresponds to only about 2.7 wt% H due to the high mass of Hf and Zr; a neutron diffraction study was not possible due to the large neutron absorption cross-section of Hf; detailed investigation of structural stability during cycling is outside the scope of this communication.. Future work: The authors suggest that much higher storage capacity by weight percent can be achieved by replacing heavy elements like Hf and Zr with lighter ones; theoretical modelling using ab initio methods is needed to explain the influence of strain on hydride stability; in situ hydrogenation details are currently being evaluated.. Quote: "reach an H/M ratio of 2.5"

card: Paper card. Question: Can the magnetocaloric properties of fully transition metal-based high entropy alloys be tuned via FCC metal additives and heat treatment to achieve a second-order magnetic phase transition with improved refrigerant capacity?. System: Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx (x = 0.00% to 11.11% atomic Pd). Processing: Arc furnace melting under argon atmosphere using 99.99% purity elements; cold rolled into sheets (100–250 μm); annealed for one hour at 900 °C in Ta foil wrapped quartz tubes with Ar gas; characterized in as-rolled and annealed states.. Test conditions: Magnetic measurements via Quantum Design PPMS with VSM option; M(H) loops from 0 to 50 kOe; isotherms from 10 K to 350 K in 5 K steps; Tc estimated at maximum dM/dT in 2 kOe field; XRD via θ–2θ with Cu Kα photons.. Findings: Tc increases monotonically from approximately 100 K (0% Pd) to 280 K (11.11% Pd) in the annealed state.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) at 5 K increases from approximately 30 emu/g to 46 emu/g with Pd addition.; Refrigerant capacity (RC) is enhanced by nearly 40% in annealed samples with less than 1.5% Pd.; Universal scaling analysis shows a decrease in the homogeneity variance statistic (F) of at least 50% with annealing or Pd incorporation.; The entropy change exponent (n) decreases toward the mean field theory prediction (2/3) with Pd addition and annealing.; The refrigerant capacity exponent (m) becomes superlinear (e.g., 1.13 for annealed 5.88% Pd) compared to the unannealed x=0 sample (0.99).; As-rolled samples show an artificial ~25% higher RC than annealed samples due to disorder broadening the exchange parameter distribution.. Mechanism: The authors argue that Pd additions and heat treatment reduce structural defects (strain, vacancies, stacking faults) and grain size reduction, leading to a reduction in the distribution of exchange energies. This homogenization of the alloy results in a more magnetically homogeneous system that exhibits behavior closer to mean field theory and a 'carat' shaped magnetic entropy change curve.. Limitations: The maximum entropy change is about a factor of 20 less than Gadolinium (Gd), and the Pd-containing alloy is ten times as expensive as Gd. The authors also note that the broadening of the entropy peak in as-rolled samples leads to an artificially enhanced refrigerant capacity that may not reflect intrinsic material performance.. Future work: The authors propose investigating other FCC metals like Cu or Ag to tune magnetism with significantly reduced material costs. They also suggest that computational materials scientists can survey the large parameter space of these alloys due to their observed mean field behavior, and recommend high-resolution neutron scattering to probe bulk structural information.. Quote: "heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy behave under plane-stress deformation (biaxial bulging) at cryogenic temperatures, and what are the underlying microstructural mechanisms?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (five-element alloy). Processing: Vacuum induction arc melting followed by homogenization annealing at 1200 °C for 24 h; hot extrusion at 950 °C with a speed of 15 mm/s and ratio of 3.01; final annealing at 950 °C for 1 h to produce thin-walled tubes; tubes cut and flattened into circular sheets (42 mm diameter) for testing.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at −160 °C and −196 °C; isothermal bulging tests at −190 °C, −140 °C, and room temperature (RT) with bulging ratios of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%; punch diameter 36 mm; minimum achievable temperature −190 °C with 1 °C accuracy.. Findings: At −196 °C, ultimate tensile strength exceeds 2100 MPa and elongation is higher than 70%.; At −160 °C, yield strength exceeds 500 MPa, ultimate tensile strength is near 1700 MPa, and elongation is approximately 60%.; Ultimate bulging heights at splitting were 12 mm for both −190 °C and −140 °C.; At −190 °C, the maximum thinning rate was 6.32%, 4.52%, 12.56%, and 10.74% smaller than at −140 °C for bulging ratios of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%, respectively.; Specimens with a bulging ratio of 25% showed the best thickness uniformity at both −190 °C and −140 °C.; The ratio of small-angle grain boundaries increased from 8.6% to 53.6% as the bulging ratio increased from 25% to 100% at −190 °C.; Average grain diameter in the original state was 8.85 μm, decreasing minimally after deformation (e.g., 8.28 μm at −190 °C).; The ratio of small-angle grain boundaries at 100% bulging ratio was 53.3% at RT, 45.9% at −140 °C, and 53.6% at −190 °C.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the simultaneous increase in strength and ductility at cryogenic temperatures is due to the appearance of nanoscale twinning, which postpones the onset of necking. For biaxial deformation, dislocation motion is identified as a main mechanism, evidenced by the significant increase in small-angle grain boundaries with increasing bulging ratio, while nanoscale twinning (difficult to observe with EBSD) may be enhanced at lower temperatures to improve plasticity.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "Both the strength and the ductility improves as the temperature decreases from −160 °C to −196 °C."

card: Paper card. Question: How do Al and C additions affect the deformation mechanisms (dislocation slip vs. twinning) and strengthening contributions during cold rolling of a CoCrFeNiMn-type high-entropy alloy compared to the equiatomic reference?. System: CoCrFeNiMn-type HEA with composition (20–23) Co, Cr, Fe, Ni; 8.82 Mn; 3.37 Al; 0.69 C (at %). Processing: Self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) in a centrifugal setup followed by induction remelting in vacuum; cold rolling unidirectionally at room temperature with reductions of 5–10% per pass to final strains of 5%, 10%, 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at an initial strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; microhardness testing with 0.3 kg load; microstructural analysis via XRD, EBSD, and TEM. Findings: Initial as-cast alloy had a coarse-grained single fcc structure with grain size of 250–400 μm and yield strength of 210 MPa.; Uniform elongation of the as-cast alloy was 74%, decreasing to 1.3% after 80% cold rolling.; Yield strength increased from 210 MPa (as-cast) to 1310 MPa after 80% rolling reduction.; Dislocation density rose from ~1 × 10¹¹ m⁻² in the as-cast condition to ~2 × 10¹⁵ m⁻² after 40% strain.; Deformation twinning onset was delayed until 20% rolling reduction, whereas the equiatomic reference showed twins after 5%.; Substructure strengthening dominated at rolling reductions <40%, while grain (twin) boundary strengthening prevailed at strains >40%.; The Al-, C-containing alloy exhibited dislocation densities approximately two times higher than the reference CoCrFeNiMn alloy at comparable strains.. Mechanism: The addition of Al and C increases the stacking fault energy (SFE), which suppresses early twinning and promotes planar dislocation slip; this results in higher dislocation density accumulation and a delayed onset of deformation twinning, shifting the dominant strengthening mechanism from substructure hardening at low strains to Hall-Petch (twin boundary) strengthening at high strains.. Limitations: The text notes that exact calculation of the SFE value is a complex problem and could not be fully evaluated due to the absence of other input values for the adapted equation, though the relative difference was confirmed via ∆Ghcp−fcc calculations.. Future work: The authors state that additional studies on the effects of alloying on deformation mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMn-type alloys are required, noting that the effect of Al is even less studied than carbon.. Quote: "The alloy with a chemical composition (at %) of (20–23) Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni; 8.82 Mn; 3.37 Al; and 0.69 C was produced by self-propagating high-temperature synthesis with subsequent induction."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti high-entropy alloy be manufactured via Directed Energy Deposition (DED) to achieve a γ + γ′ phase structure that enhances thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength compared to typical FCC-structured HEAs?. System: Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA (45.0 at% Ni, 20.0 at% Co, 10.0 at% Fe, 10.0 at% Cr, 7.5 at% Al, 7.5 at% Ti) deposited on SUS 304 substrates. Processing: Direct Energy Deposition (DED) using a 2 kW diode laser (980 nm, 3 mm beam diameter) with a laser velocity of 10 mm/s, powder feed rate of 7 g/min, hatch spacing of 1 mm, and 11 layers; powders (45 and 150 μm) mixed for 4 hours; nitrogen carrier gas used to prevent oxidation. Test conditions: Room temperature (20 °C) tensile testing per ASTM E8/E8M-18 standard on specimens with 4.5 mm thickness; microhardness measured via Vickers tester with 5 readings per height; XRD (Cu radiation, 40 kV, 50 mA) and EBSD analysis performed. Findings: The alloy exhibited a γ + γ′ phase structure with an ordered FCC (L12) γ′ phase confirmed by XRD superlattice peaks.; Yield strength was measured at 514 MPa and ultimate tensile strength at 605 MPa (631 MPa in conclusions).; Microhardness was consistent at approximately 370 HV across the deposited height.; The average grain size of the γ phase was coarse, measured at 116 μm.; The γ′ phase composition was identified as (Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al) via EDS analysis.; No secondary precipitated phases other than γ + γ′ were detected in the microstructure.; The hardness exceeded that of wrought Inconel 718 (350 HV).. Mechanism: The addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within the multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, where the ordered FCC γ′ phase significantly improves mechanical properties, thermal stability, and coarsening resistance.. Limitations: The tensile strength is lower than Inconel 718 due to the coarsening of the microstructure caused by high-temperature deposition, and the grain size distribution is uneven due to variations in processing parameters and cooling rates.. Future work: Post-processing treatments like heat treatment are expected to refine the phase size and improve mechanical properties; precise phase analysis and post-treatment procedures should be added to further advance the manufacturing method.. Quote: "The γ′ phase with an ordered FCC structure significantly improves the mechanical properties."

card: Paper card. Question: How do simultaneous microalloying with carbon (C) and molybdenum (Mo) affect the microstructure evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties of Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloys?. System: [Co40Cr25(FeNi)35−yMoy]100−xCx (x = 0, 0.5; y = 3, 4, 5 at.%) HEAs. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of pure elements (≥99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, melted five times for homogeneity, solution treated at 1200 °C for 2 h, water quenched, and hot rolled with 70% reduction. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; XRD (20° to 100°, 40 kV, 40 mA); SEM and EBSD analysis. Findings: Without carbon, alloys exhibited an FCC + HCP dual-phase structure, whereas adding 0.5 at.% C resulted in a single FCC phase.; In non-carbon alloys, grain size increased from 17 μm to 47 μm as Mo content rose from 3 to 5 at.%.; The Mo4C0.5 alloy showed a significant decrease in grain size compared to other compositions after carbon addition.; In the Mo5C0.5 alloy, Mo content exceeded the solid solution limit, leading to the formation of Mo carbides.; The Mo4C0.5 alloy achieved a yield strength of 757 MPa, tensile strength of 1186 MPa, and elongation of 69%.; Carbon addition increased the yield strength of the alloys by 99 MPa, 54 MPa, and 105 MPa compared to non-carbon counterparts.; Deformation mechanism shifted from TRIP (FCC to HCP) in non-carbon alloys to TWIP (twinning) in carbon-containing alloys.. Mechanism: The superior mechanical properties of the Mo4C0.5 alloy are attributed to a combination of fine grain strengthening, interstitial solid solution strengthening from carbon, precipitation strengthening from carbides, and the TWIP effect where deformation twins hinder dislocation slip, delay necking, and enhance work hardening.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The Mo4C0.5 HEA exhibited excellent comprehensive mechanical properties, which was superior to a majority of reported HEAs and conventional metal alloys."
